initial_presentation: A 14-year-old male presented to the neurogenetics outpatient clinic in a wheelchair, with a history of progressive disabilities over eight years. He was born at full term via vaginal delivery without complications. At six years old, he developed tremors in his right hand during activities such as writing or eating. By age seven, the tremors worsened, and he exhibited a staggering gait and slow reactions. Concurrently, he experienced speech difficulties, including slurred pronunciation and slow speech. At nine years old, he developed difficulty swallowing and occasionally coughed while drinking water. His speech and coordination issues continued to deteriorate, requiring assistance for walking. At age 12, he began experiencing painful walking spasms, increased ataxia, and more severe speech difficulties, with occasional falls. He also became irritable, cried frequently, sweated excessively at the extremities, and developed urinary incontinence.

A 63-year-old man was readmitted to our hospital for further evaluation of a hepatic cystic lesion. One year prior, he experienced pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen and fever, leading to a visit to a local hospital. An abdominal sonogram revealed a cystic lesion approximately 10 cm in size in the right lobe of the liver, and pus-like material was aspirated. He was then referred to our hospital for further management. Upon admission, his temperature was 38.0°C, pulse 80 per minute, respiration 20 per minute, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a primary concern of retained deciduous teeth. Physical examination showed short stature, prominent frontal and parietal regions, a depressed nasal bridge, a beaked nose, underdeveloped midface, an obtuse mandibular gonial angle with relative prognathism, wrinkled skin over the fingertips, and nail abnormalities. Intraoral examination identified a deep midline antero-posterior ridge of the palate, a high arched palate, multiple retained deciduous teeth with caries, crowding, and enamel hypoplasia.

A 10-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of neurodevelopmental delay. She was the first child of consanguineous parents (second cousins), born full term by cesarean section without any birth complications. Her birth weight was 2700 grams and her head circumference was 35 cm. During the physical and neurological examination, motor development assessment revealed the ability to roll over, but head control was incomplete. Head nodding was observed. She exhibited hypotonicity and did not bear weight when held in a vertical position. Pendular bilateral nystagmus was noted since the neonatal period. There was no history of seizures.

The patient is a two-year-old girl born at full term to consanguineous Saudi parents via cesarean section due to breech presentation. She has a history of poor sucking, hypotonia, bilateral ptosis, and recurrent admissions to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for apnea. The family history is unremarkable. The clinical course began with a sudden cessation of breathing lasting more than 15 minutes, followed by a three-minute arrest. She also has a history of choking and coughing. Upon examination, the patient was afebrile, dehydrated, and pale, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3.

A 4-year-old boy, firstborn to third-degree consanguineous parents of north Indian origin, exhibited progressive spasticity in the lower limbs and regression of motor milestones starting at 1 year of age. The antenatal and perinatal periods were uncomplicated, and there were no affected family members. He achieved motor, adaptive, social, and language milestones appropriately until 1 year of age. Prior to the onset of symptoms, he could walk with one handheld, had a mature pincer grasp, waved bye-bye, and spoke two meaningful words. Initially, he experienced gait instability, toe walking, and frequent falls without diurnal fluctuation. By 2 years of age, he ceased walking and had significant difficulty standing independently, with a crouch at the knee. He also developed tightness in the bilateral lower limbs at the knee and ankle. Despite slower progress compared to peers, he continued to gain social and language milestones. At 4 years old, he had a vocabulary of 10–20 words and could indicate bowel and bladder needs but required assistance. He had difficulty with fine motor tasks in the upper limbs and slurred speech. Examination revealed Ashworth grade III spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, and dynamic flexion contractures at the ankles in the lower limbs. In the upper limbs, there was grade I spasticity, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and spastic dysarthria. Anthropometry and physical examination were otherwise normal.

A 7-year-old girl experienced upper abdominal pain after lunch, leading to early dismissal from school on three occasions over the past 10 days. She also had a low-grade fever and indigestion in the days leading up to her visit. Physical examination revealed slight tenderness in the right upper quadrant upon deep palpation, consistent with Murphy's sign.

A 33-year-old African American male presented with multiple nodular skin lesions, primarily located in the axilla and inguinal areas. He reported an increase in the number and size of draining pustules. The patient also experienced generalized joint pains, including swelling and redness in the left knee and right elbow.

A 64-year-old female patient presented with a primary concern of a painless swelling in the mouth persisting for 1 year. Intraoral examination identified a moderately firm, well-defined, ovoid, solitary swelling in the left sublingual region, measuring approximately 3 cm × 2 cm. The swelling was mobile upon bimanual palpation. An occlusal view showed no signs of erosion or bony destruction of adjacent structures.

A 55-year-old African man visited the ophthalmologist due to a growth on his right upper eyelid that had been present for 8 months. The swelling began at the orbital ridge and extended to the entire upper lid. The patient reported spontaneous bleeding from the lesion, eye discharge, and rashes before the visit. He was unable to fully open the affected eye. There was no history of trauma, photophobia, weight loss, or tearing. The patient had undergone surgery and chemotherapy for rectal carcinoma 6 years ago, with the last chemotherapy session 5 years prior to this visit. He has a known history of asthma and no family history of similar conditions. On examination, the right eye showed a projecting fleshy mass on the upper eyelid, measuring 3.3 × 2.0 cm. The mass was firm, lobulated, and nontender with irregular rough surfaces. Additionally, there was a mildly tender, mobile, nonmatted right preauricular lymph node.
